items_missed: Save Your Ass speech never happened — 0/10. Not one word about prep before move day shortening the move and lowering the bill, no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload' tip, no 'does that make sense?' close. On a time-billed job where the customer opened with 'calling just to get just to see if I can afford you' and later said 'unless we can strike something I can afford' and 'I might have to hire high-school boys,' this is the single largest miss on the call.

Actively coached AGAINST prep. When she volunteered 'I would probably take his drawers out so I don't have to unload them,' Erik answered 'You can leave the stuff in there if you'd like we'll move it as it is.' Technically true, but on a $204/hr clock he talked a budget-anxious customer out of the exact behavior that shortens her move. She also volunteered the carload tip herself — 'the little things, we'll just take the pickup over the weekend' — and he never reinforced or built on it.

No Worries Damage Coverage never named and the $2,000 figure never given. She handed him the opening twice: 'the painters got a hold of it last week' and 'they had it moved on top of each other with things in between and it was gouges and holes, and it was just awful.' His answer was 'we have a really, really good insurance policy in place' — the concept without the name, the dollar limit, or the 60¢/lb baseline contrast. Partial credit only.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned — despite the customer explicitly asking for it in her own words twice: 'I just like to see what the truck looks like' and 'so I'll know when it's coming up the road,' plus 'do you have any references around here.' A textbook setup, unused.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned at all.

No booking attempt. He built the scarcity — 'I have two trucks that are open... I can't necessarily guarantee that those spots will still be there... first come, first served' — and then never asked for the business. He closed with 'give us a holler when you read everything over. If this sounds like something you're willing to commit to... just reach out to us.' A 43-minute call, a warm buyer who said 'it's looking good to me,' and no ask.

Estimate is almost certainly light and was never revised as the inventory grew. He quoted 3.5–4.5 hours with 2 movers early, then she kept adding: upright piano, 3-piece curved sectional, two recliners, king adjustable bed with two mattresses, big dresser, chest of drawers, antique hutch, trundle bed, washer and dryer, dining table plus buffet plus a second hutch, breakfast/game table with five rolling chairs, two display corner units, a patio swing requiring disassembly, two more dressers, two desks, a serving cart — plus a possible storage stop. The 3.5–4.5 hour number was never touched. Direct hit on the estimate-accuracy rock.

Pricing range stated inconsistently and confusingly. He said 3.5 hrs = $714 and 4.5 hrs = $918, then summarized 'that's kind of where I'm at right now is somewhere between the $714 and 510 range' — mixing the high end, the low end, and the 2.5-hour minimum into one sentence. She had to ask '714 and what?' to get it re-read.

Talking too fast, called out twice by the customer. 'I have a hearing problem and my hearing aid can't keep up with people who talk real fast... if you could just slow down a little bit' and then again mid-pricing: 'Okay, Eric you're getting too fast again.' He apologized both times ('I apologize', 'Oh, sorry. Where should I go back to?') and relapsed. On an 88-year-old with a stated hearing aid, pace is the accessibility issue on this call.

The 'no hidden fees' pitch landed backwards and took three passes to repair. 'Outside of the hourly rate. There are no additional fees or hidden fees of any type' was heard as a charge — 'Now wait a minute. You said you just said that's outside of the hourly rate' and 'you're saying outside 204 sounds like you're charging extra for that.' He recovered, but the word 'outside' broke the differentiator. Say 'included' first, then 'nothing else on top.'

15-minute prorated increments after the minimum never explained. She got the clock start, the clock stop, and the 2.5-hour minimum, but not how time is billed between the tiers — which is exactly what she was trying to compute when she asked 'you won't know how much, how long, how much time it's gonna take until it's all done, right?'

No 'does that make sense?' sense-check anywhere — not after pricing, not after the clock, not after the estimate, and not even after the hidden-fees confusion he had just spent three exchanges untangling.
Never asked 'how are you today?' and never asked for confirmation on the agenda ('sound good?').

No street address captured for either location — he asked, then accepted zip only ('or I guess if you have a zip code for, for either of those that would also work'). Both ends are 75069 but she volunteered 'I live in Fairview and they let us use their zip code,' and she also volunteered 'I am in a gated community, so you'll have to have a little extra time to get through there.' No addresses means no real drive-time or access planning on a quote she is about to receive in writing.

The storage stop was never resolved. She raised it four separate times ('might wind up having to take it to the storage instead of over there', 'we may have to make another truck to the storage place'). He priced the concept correctly but never got the storage facility address, never asked whether to build it into the estimate, and never asked what is going there.

Never asked about packing services — on a customer who said 'I've got to get rid of some of this stuff,' 'I'm the one that's slowing them down cause I can't get everything done,' and 'I need to take about a month off.' A packing add-on was the obvious solve for her actual problem and was never offered.
No Sparefoot referral despite three separate storage mentions, and no Ecobox mention.

Never asked about additional rooms (garage, attic, shed) or access concerns (apartment parking, elevator, carry distance, HOA). She surfaced the patio, the closet dresser, and the gated community herself; he acknowledged the gate with 'that's totally fine' and moved on.

Never asked the moving-stressor question. She broadcast the stressors unprompted — 88 years old, no sleep, no-show cleaners, damaged heirloom furniture, affordability — and he answered them warmly but never asked 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?', which is what would have surfaced the top concern to log on the job.

Piano handled as an inventory line, not a variable. He logged 'upright piano' and explained weight limits (350 lb upstairs, 600 lb flat ground) but never explained that a piano adds time or needs special handling — and never revisited whether 2 movers is right for a piano plus a curved sectional plus a king adjustable bed.
No walk-distance discussion and no equivalents (school bus reference) used, on a house-to-apartment move where apartment carry distance is a primary time driver.

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'any other questions before I let you go?' — she drove every question herself, right through 'do you want money on the front?' at the very end of the call, which is how the no-deposit differentiator finally came out.
top_strength: Rapport, and it was genuinely excellent. Erik turned a 43-minute call with an exhausted 88-year-old into something she enjoyed — she told him so twice: 'Oh! You're so nice' and 'it's been a pleasure.' He caught the piano line perfectly: when she said 'you'd hate to see this 88 year old woman out there lifting a piano,' he answered 'You're absolutely right. I would be very upset if somebody let you do that,' and then 'if we can help you, I'd rather that than have you out there doing the back breaking work yourself.' He found real common ground on the military and geography — 'I'm originally from North Carolina I grew up in Virginia now. I live in Fort Worth' against her Fort Bragg and Virginia history — and when she mentioned her husband didn't make it, he said 'Sorry to hear that' rather than steamrolling. He validated her 60-year-old furniture with 'that's when they used to make stuff good quality nowadays they sure don't,' gave her 'washers can be pretty beefy' (she laughed: 'That's a good word for it'), reassured her through her own self-criticism with 'Oh, don't say that miss Anne' and 'you're doing great. I'll say you're this is, this has been a very enjoyable call for me,' and noticed she hadn't eaten — 'Oh, my goodness! It's 2:00. You better eat something.' He also handled two non-standard asks honestly and helpfully: the certificate of insurance ('If you request a certificate of insurance, I can pull one for you and get that over to you') and the reviews question, where he declined to invent a reference list and pointed her to real reviews instead. Used 'miss Anne' throughout, and the structure was there — 'explain the pricing structure... then how our clock works and lastly the estimate' — a clean mid-call agenda most reps skip.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is not subtle: this customer told Erik her problem in the first two minutes — 'calling just to get just to see if I can afford you' — and he never gave her a single way to spend less. The Save Your Ass speech is the whole answer to her call and it scored 0/10. The moment to run it was when she said 'I would probably take his drawers out so I don't have to unload them.' He said 'You can leave the stuff in there if you'd like we'll move it as it is.' What he needed to say: 'Miss Anne, actually — do take them out, and here's why. We bill by time, so every minute we save is money back in your pocket. Anything you and your son can carry in the pickup over the weekend, take it. Empty the dresser drawers, pull the photos off the walls, box up the loose stuff, and get the patio and the gym equipment cleared before we arrive. Do that and I'd expect us closer to the three-and-a-half-hour end at $714 than the four-and-a-half at $918. Does that make sense?' That one paragraph converts her stated anxiety into a lower bill, an accurate estimate, and a booking. Second fix: slow down. She asked twice — 'my hearing aid can't keep up with people who talk real fast' and 'Eric you're getting too fast again' — and he apologized and sped back up. Third: ask for the business. He built the scarcity ('I have two trucks that are open... first come, first served') and then handed her the exit: 'give us a holler when you read everything over.' The line was 'I've got two trucks open Monday and I can hold one for you right now — no deposit, and it's free to move or cancel if the apartment isn't ready. Nothing to lose. Want me to put you down?' She was ready; she said 'it's looking good to me.' Fourth: she gave him the Meet Your Mover cue verbatim — 'I just like to see what the truck looks like... so I'll know when it's coming up the road' — and the No Worries cue twice with the painter story. Both differentiators go in that exact spot: 'A few days before the move we email you your mover's photo and info so you know exactly who's pulling up. And after what the painters did — that's what No Worries Damage Coverage is for: up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage.' Estimate-accuracy note for the rock file: this is a textbook case of a quote fixed early and never revisited. He priced 3.5–4.5 hours with 2 movers, and she then added roughly twenty more items including a piano, a curved sectional, an adjustable king, a washer and dryer, three case-goods pieces from a dining room, a disassembly-required patio swing, and a possible storage stop — and the number never moved. Before the estimate email goes out, that job needs a re-quote, a decision on the storage stop, and both street addresses. Also add the certificate of insurance he committed to sending and confirm it is actually logged.
phone_presence_notes: Genuine warmth end to end — consistent 'miss Anne,' real humor she reciprocated ('washers can be pretty beefy' / 'That's a good word for it'), a found military-and-geography connection, empathy at the piano and the deceased-husband moments, and a customer who volunteered 'Oh! You're so nice' and 'Eric, you make a good sell' and stayed engaged for 43 minutes.
audio_review_reason: Speaking pace is the one coachable on this call and it cannot be judged from text — the customer flagged it twice ('my hearing aid can't keep up with people who talk real fast' and 'Eric you're getting too fast again'), so audio is needed to confirm how fast he was actually going, whether he slowed after each request, and how much of the hidden-fees confusion was pace versus wording. Erik's transcript also has scattered garbled fragments and cut-in overlaps that may indicate talk-over rather than a clean handoff.
